## Overview

The Santee were a historic tribe of Native Americans who lived in South Carolina, primarily along the Santee River in the counties of Clarendon and Orangeburg. Their settlements were centered near the area of the present-day town of Santee, South Carolina. The river settlement was later dammed and is now called Lake Marion. The Santee were a small tribe even during the early eighteenth century. In 1715, a census recorded two villages containing forty-three men. The Santee language is sparsely preserved, but scholars including John R. Swanton maintained that it belonged to the Siouan-Catawban language family. Frank Speck connected the name Santee with *iswaⁿ´ti*, a Catawban expression meaning “the river” or “the river is there.” The Santee are significant in the sources for their river-valley settlements, distinctive governance, burial customs, clothing, storage buildings, and documented encounters with English colonists.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe clothing and adornment. Distinguished members of the Santee wore robes made from feathers. Other garments and sashes were often woven from animal hair. The account of Simon Flowers records that he had facial tattoos and said that his siblings had also received tattoos from their father during childhood.

### Architecture

The sources describe several forms of Santee settlement and construction. In 1675, Captain Maurice Mathews directed the Santee to establish a town on the banks of Wadboo Creek, across the Cooper River. In 1700, John Lawson described Santee towns, which he called plantations, extending for many miles along the Santee River. Lawson also recorded a village called Hickerau, or Black House, near modern Summerton, South Carolina, and described temporary hunting encampments.

Santee provision houses were raised on posts and coated with clay. These structures were used to store corn, and the practice was shared with several other Southeastern tribes. Santee rulers were buried on mounds built according to their status, with a roof supported by poles sheltering the graves.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They do record facial tattoos. Simon Flowers, described in an October 26, 1766 notice in the South Carolina Gazette as an American Indian or Mustee born at Santee River, had distinctive facial tattoos. He stated that his siblings had also been tattooed by their father during childhood.

## Music & performance

They do record a spoken eulogy in connection with funerary practice. After the death of ordinary tribe members, their remains were left exposed on a platform for several days, while a close relative with a blackened face recited a eulogy.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document burial customs and a religious practice connected with the moon. Santee rulers were interred atop mounds constructed according to their status, beneath a roof supported by poles. After the death of other members, their remains were exposed on a platform for several days. A close relative with a blackened face recited a eulogy. The bones were later wrapped in possum fur cloth and annually cleaned and oiled. Some Santee families retained ancestral bones for multiple generations.

Thomas Ashe, reporting on South Carolina in 1682 under commission of the King of England, described Santee religious beliefs as centered on the adoration of the sun and moon. He reported that, at the appearance of the new moon, tribal members extended and folded their arms and inclined their bodies in worship.

## Foodways

They do state that the Santee stored corn in provision houses raised on posts and coated with clay. This indicates the importance of corn storage in the material organization of the settlement. John Lawson also described a hunter and his wife among the people he encountered, as well as temporary hunting encampments between Hickerau and the High Hills of Santee.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not preserve Santee folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or a named literary tradition. They do record historical accounts and spoken forms associated with Santee life. John Lawson reported meeting the King of the Santee, the chief doctor, a hunter, and his wife during his visit in 1700. In funerary practice, a close relative recited a eulogy beside the exposed remains of a deceased person.

## Language & religion

Few words of the Santee language have been preserved. John R. Swanton and other scholars maintained that the tribe spoke a Siouan-Catawban language. Frank Speck suggested that the name Santee derived from *iswaⁿ´ti*, a Catawban expression glossed as “the river” or “the river is there.” The Santee have sometimes been confused with the Santee Sioux because of the similarity of their names, although the Santee Sioux were described as another Siouan-Catawban-speaking people situated primarily within the Dakotas, Minnesota, and Manitoba, Canada.

Thomas Ashe’s 1682 account described Santee religious beliefs as focused on the adoration of the sun and moon. At the appearance of the new moon, he witnessed tribal members worshipping with extended and folded arms and inclined bodies.
